rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: When \(\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4}\) is fused with \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) in the presence of air it gives a yellow solution of compound (A). Compound (A) on acidification gives compound (B). Compound (B) on reaction with \(\mathrm{KCl}\) forms an orange coloured (C). An acidified solution of compound (C) oxidises iodide to (D). Identify (A), (B), (C) and (D).
rows.solution:
This is the industrial route from chromite ore to potassium dichromate, and each colour named in the question is the clue.

Fusing chromite with sodium carbonate in air oxidises the chromium from \(+3\) to \(+6\), and the YELLOW solution is the chromate:
\(4\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4} + 8\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 7\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 8\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 8\mathrm{CO_2}\)
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\), sodium chromate

Acidification converts chromate to dichromate; chromium stays at \(+6\), so this is not a redox change:
\(2\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7}\), sodium dichromate

Potassium chloride exchanges the cation, and the much less soluble potassium salt crystallises out ORANGE:
\(\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\), potassium dichromate

Acidified dichromate is a strong oxidising agent and takes iodide to iodine:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 6\mathrm{I^-} + 14\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{I_2} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{D} = \mathrm{I_2}\), iodine

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) The melting points of \(\alpha\)-amino acids are generally higher than that of the corresponding carboxylic acids.
(b) Amino acids show amphoteric behaviour.
rows.solution:
(a) An \(\alpha\)-amino acid does not exist as the neutral molecule the formula suggests. Its \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group transfers its proton to its own \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group, giving a DIPOLAR ION, the zwitterion \(\mathrm{H_3\overset{+}{N}-CHR-COO^-}\). The solid is therefore held together by strong electrostatic attraction between full positive and full negative charges, much as an ionic salt is, rather than by the weaker hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces holding a carboxylic acid together. Far more energy is needed to break that lattice, so the melting points are much higher.

(b) Because the zwitterion carries both an acidic and a basic centre. In the presence of a base the \(-\mathrm{\overset{+}{N}H_3}\) group gives up a proton, so the amino acid behaves as an acid; in the presence of an acid the \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\) group accepts a proton, so it behaves as a base. Having both functional groups in the same molecule is what makes amino acids amphoteric.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: A solution containing 15 g urea (molar mass = 60 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) per litre of solution in water has the same osmotic pressure (isotonic) as a solution of glucose (molar mass = 180 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) in water. Calculate the mass of glucose present in one litre of its solution.
rows.solution:
Isotonic solutions have equal osmotic pressures, and at the same temperature that means equal MOLAR concentrations:
\(\Pi = CRT \implies C_{\text{glucose}} = C_{\text{urea}}\)

Writing each concentration as moles per litre,
\(\dfrac{w_G}{M_G} = \dfrac{w_U}{M_U} \implies \dfrac{w_G}{180} = \dfrac{15}{60}\)

\(w_G = \dfrac{15 \times 180}{60} = 45\ \mathrm{g}\)

So 45 g of glucose per litre. Note that three times the mass is needed for the same osmotic pressure, because glucose's molar mass is three times urea's — a colligative property counts particles, not grams.

rows.stem:
Calculate \(\Delta_r \mathrm{G^{\circ}}\) and log \(\mathrm{K_C}\) of the reaction :
\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq) + Ag^{+}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq) + Ag(s)}\)
Given \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Ag^{+}/Ag}} = 0.80\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}} = 0.77\) V
[R = 8.314 J \(\mathrm{K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)]
rows.solution:
The silver couple has the higher reduction potential, so it is the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}} = 0.80 - 0.77 = 0.03\ \mathrm{V}\)

One electron is transferred in the reaction as written, so \(n = 1\):
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell} = -1 \times 96500 \times 0.03 = -2895\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)
that is \(-2.895\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

The equilibrium constant follows from
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2.303\,RT\log K_C\)
\(\log K_C = \dfrac{-\Delta_r G^{\circ}}{2.303\,RT} = \dfrac{2895}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298} = \dfrac{2895}{5700}\)
\(\log K_C = 0.508\)

A small positive \(\log K_C\) is what a cell potential of only \(0.03\) V should give: the reaction is spontaneous, but barely.

rows.stem:
(a) Arrange the following in decreasing order of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) :
Aniline, p-nitroaniline, p-methylaniline
(b) Account for the following :
(i) Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are more stable than those of aliphatic amines.
(ii) Methylamine in water reacts with \(\mathrm{FeCl_3}\) to precipitate hydrated ferric oxide.
rows.solution:
(a) A HIGHER \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a WEAKER base, so decreasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means listing the weakest base first. All three have nitrogen attached directly to the ring, so what separates them is the substituent para to it. The nitro group withdraws electron density both inductively and by resonance, pulling the lone pair further away and making p-nitroaniline much the weakest base. The methyl group releases electron density, making p-methylaniline the strongest. Aniline, with no substituent, lies between.

Decreasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\): p-nitroaniline \(>\) aniline \(>\) p-methylaniline.

(b)(i) Because of resonance. In an aryl diazonium ion the positive charge is delocalised into the benzene ring, which spreads it out and stabilises the ion enough for the salt to be isolated at low temperature. An aliphatic diazonium ion has no such delocalisation: it expels nitrogen immediately to give a carbocation, which is why aliphatic diazonium salts cannot be kept.

(ii) Methylamine is a base, so in water it takes a proton from a water molecule and releases hydroxide ions:
\(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3\overset{+}{N}H_3} + \mathrm{OH^-}\)
Those hydroxide ions then precipitate iron(III) from the ferric chloride solution as hydrated ferric oxide:
\(2\mathrm{FeCl_3} + 6\mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O} + 6\mathrm{Cl^-}\)
The amine itself does not react with the iron; it acts only by generating hydroxide.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the reaction when D-glucose reacts with the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{NH_2OH}\)
(ii) Acetic anhydride
(b) Why vitamin C cannot be stored in our body ?
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Hydroxylamine condenses with the free aldehyde group at C-1, losing water, to give glucose oxime:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{NH_2OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH{=}N-OH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
This reaction is evidence for the carbonyl group in the open chain form.

(ii) Acetic anhydride acetylates every hydroxyl group, and glucose has five — four secondary and one primary — so the product is glucose pentaacetate:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)
This is the reaction that establishes how many hydroxyl groups the molecule carries.

(b) Vitamin C is WATER soluble. The body cannot store water-soluble vitamins: any amount beyond immediate need dissolves in the body fluids and is excreted in the urine. That is why vitamin C must be supplied regularly in the diet, whereas the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue.

rows.stem:
For the complex \(\mathrm{[Fe(en)_2Cl_2]\ Cl}\), identify :
(a) the oxidation number of iron.
(b) the hybridization and the shape of the complex.
(c) the magnetic behaviour of the complex
(d) whether there is an optical isomer of the complex ? If so draw its structure.
(e) IUPAC name of the complex.
(At. no. of Fe = 26)
rows.solution:
(a) One chloride sits outside the coordination sphere and carries \(-1\), so the complex cation is \(+1\). Inside it the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are neutral and the two chlorido ligands contribute \(-1\) each, so iron must be \(+3\).
Oxidation number of iron: \(+3\)

(b) \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\). Ethane-1,2-diamine is a strong enough field ligand to force pairing, so the five d electrons crowd into the lower set, freeing two \(3d\) orbitals for bonding.
Hybridisation: \(d^2sp^3\); shape: octahedral.

(c) That pairing leaves ONE electron unpaired, so the complex is paramagnetic.

(d) Yes. The complex exists as cis and trans geometrical isomers, and of these only the CIS form lacks a plane of symmetry. The cis isomer is therefore chiral and exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images — two optical isomers.

In the cis form the two chlorido ligands occupy adjacent positions of the octahedron and the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands span the remaining four, each chelating across a pair of adjacent positions. The mirror image of that arrangement cannot be rotated onto the original, which is what makes it optically active. The trans isomer, with the two chlorides opposite each other, has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

(e) Ligands are cited alphabetically, chlorido before ethane-1,2-diamine, and since the ligand name contains numerals the multiplying prefix is bis:
dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)iron(III) chloride

rows.stem:
(a) Using IUPAC norms write the names of the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4\ Cl(NO_2)]Cl}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\)
(b) What is crystal field splitting energy ? Why low spin tetrahedral complexes are not formed ?
rows.solution:
(a)(i) One chloride outside contributes \(-1\), so the cation is \(+1\); inside, four neutral ammine ligands, one chlorido at \(-1\) and one nitrito at \(-1\) put cobalt at \(+3\). The \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) written with nitrogen first means the ligand is bound through nitrogen, shown as nitrito-N. Alphabetical order gives ammine, chlorido, nitrito:
tetraamminechloridonitrito-N-cobalt(III) chloride

(ii) Three potassium ions contribute \(+3\), so the complex anion is \(-3\); six cyanido ligands at \(-1\) each put iron at \(+3\), and an anionic complex takes the Latin stem with the \(-ate\) ending:
potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)

(iii) Three oxalate ligands contribute \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so chromium is \(+3\). The species is an ion and is named as such:
trioxalatochromate(III) ion

(b) Crystal field splitting energy is the difference in energy between the two sets of d orbitals produced when the ligands approach the metal — \(\Delta_0\) between \(t_{2g}\) and \(e_g\) in an octahedral field. Before the ligands arrive the five d orbitals are degenerate; the ligands, treated as point charges, raise the energy of those orbitals pointing towards them more than the others, and the gap that opens is the splitting energy.

Low spin tetrahedral complexes are not formed because that gap is too small in a tetrahedral field. Only four ligands approach, and none head-on along an orbital axis, so \(\Delta_t\) works out at about four-ninths of \(\Delta_0\) for the same ligands. It is therefore almost always LESS than the energy needed to pair two electrons in one orbital, so the electrons spread out rather than pair and the complex is high spin.
